title: The Marxist Who Foresaw the AI Bubble
author: Ted Reese
content:
![The Marxist Who Foresaw the AI
Bubble](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-7.29.55
---AM-1.png)

Like the 2020s, the "Roaring Twenties" of a century ago witnessed a
technological revolution: The rise of the automobile, widespread
electrification, and mass production had all transformed everyday life. In his
[_speech_](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/address-accepting-the-
republican-presidential-nomination-stanford-california?ref=compactmag.com)
accepting the Republican presidential nomination in 1928, Herbert Hoover
declared that America was closer than any society in history to the "final
triumph over poverty." But trouble was brewing.

Beginning in 1926, a little-known Polish political economist named Henryk
Grossman gave a series of lectures at the University of Frankfurt in which he
argued that the era's great productive forces had been built on a fatally
unstable foundation. While America's material prosperity was real, much of its
enviable monetary fortune was in fact fictitious. Profits were not growing
fast enough to keep pace with the ever-greater amount of capital seeking a
return. Following the figures closely, he
[_noticed_](https://www.amazon.com/Law-Accumulation-Breakdown-Capitalist-
System-ebook/dp/B077L71R2L?ref=compactmag.com) that in 1927, "industry and
commerce have watched their production fall, their sales decline, and their
profits contract," even as bank deposits swelled. Capital was instead flowing
into speculation in stocks and real estate. The United States felt as if it
were whizzing toward the peak of the mountain, when it was actually about to
slam into it at full speed.

In his well-timed _The Law of Accumulation and Breakdown of the Capitalist
System_ , which appeared just months before the Wall Street crash of 1929,
Grossman argued that the reason for the problem he had identified was simple.
Each wave of mechanization allows firms to produce more with fewer workers,
cheapening goods and allowing the most efficient to win out against
competitors. But this also ties up more and more capital in machinery. Output
soars while average returns sink lower and lower. Eventually, there is more
capital seeking profitable outlets than production can absorb, and the excess
spills into speculation. This is why the money wealth of the 1920s was
perilously fictitious. It consisted of claims on future profits that the real
economy would never generate.
